doc.title: George Benson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: A&M records, Creed Taylor's control and meeting Chet Atkins
summary: Working out the discography, Benson recalls the A&M albums, Creed Taylor's control of material, and Chattanooga Choo-Choo. He became friends with Chet Atkins and recorded Sunrise in his studio.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Okay. Your association with CTI is the one that got you into – because it’s CTI records, it didn’t have the distribution, I’m sure, that everyone wanted, but . . .
Well, at first it was A&M Records. We didn’t sell a lot of records, because . . .
Right. The Other Side of Abbey Road?
The first record was called . . .
That came later.
No. Go back to A&M.
Unfortunately, that’s one of the things that’s wrong here . . .
Oh, okay.
. . . is that they have foregrounded and put in . . .

There was a picture of me on the cover, like I was being born. One of my friends had to explain that to me later. I had no idea what they were trying to do with these labels, these record companies. But it was called . . .
Body Talk is . . .
Beyond the Blue Horizon.
Beyond the Blue Horizon. Excuse me. That’s right.
Beyond the Blue Horizon, and then we did – the second album I think was – no. Beyond the Blue Horizon was the first record with Creed Taylor. There’s some before that.
The Other Side of Abbey Road is on A&M.
Yes. That’s the second record that we did.
Okay. Then this discography is missing . . .
We did one before that.
Unfortunately this goes from Verve to A&M. I’ll do some research while we go. So, A&M. How did that turn for A&M into CTI then?
When Creed couldn’t come up with the big smashes anymore, he had a falling out with Herb Alpert, or the record company, I should say.
Shape of Things?

That’s it. The Shape of Things to Come. They had a picture of me half-naked on there. Creed Taylor was telling me, this is what’s going to be happening next. The Shape of Things to Come. We did some very commercial-sounding things, but they did allow me to rip a few things. But the world wasn’t ready for that yet, not from my point of view.
Okay. But you got to choose the material? Or was this a collaboration?

Some of it. No, Creed was – he was in charge. There were a lot of things that went on that I didn’t particularly – I wasn’t particularly fond of, but I was so happy to be in an environment where people knew what they were doing – I’m talking about, who had the same goal that I had, finding an audience. There were a few things on there I really liked. Chattanooga Choo-choo. It made me famous among country people. The country guitar players love that stuff. They still remember that stuff. When I went – I started playing down at the Grand Ole Opry and places like that in the South . . .
Did you ever meet Chet Atkins?
Him and I became the best of friends.
I figured that would be the case.
We did, and we recorded a fantastic song together that I partially wrote, called Sunrise. You got to hear that song. Have you heard that, Sunrise? [Unidentified]: No, I haven’t.
You got to hear the song called Sunrise. We recorded it in Chet Atkins’s studio. Anyway, we were talking about what?
